Source Title: Literature Review on Needs of Upper Limb Prosthesis Users
Main Topic Area: Multiple (user needs/satisfaction; control interfaces; sensory feedback; evaluation/abandonment)[3]
Key Gaps Identified: Heterogeneous methods/tools make systematic comparison difficult[3]; lack of common evaluation criteria for user satisfaction/usefulness[3]; limited analysis of bilateral user needs[3]; many solutions remain research-only without clinical application[3]; pattern recognition needs long training and performs differently in real-world vs lab settings[3].
Key Limitations Discussed: Current devices often lack an intuitive, reliable interface to map user intent to prosthesis movement[3]; long training and signal degradation due to sweating/socket positioning issues[3]; invasive intraneural electrodes have high invasiveness and signal degeneration from fibrotic reaction[3]; lack of sensory feedback and actuator noise leave users' needs unmet[3]; studies vary in analysis methods/user selection and are often single-site/country (limited generalizability)[3].
Key Recommendations: Use design inputs to increase satisfaction and reduce abandonment[3]; introduce a common evaluation scale for prosthetic usefulness (e.g., Likert)[3]; conduct in-depth analysis of bilateral user needs/priorities[3]; integrate tactile sensorization (contact, sliding, temperature, force)[3] and develop control that independently manages finger position and force[3].
Contradictions Or Debates: Tension: myoelectric prostheses can be more dexterous/intuitive[3], yet users still prioritize missing sensory feedback[3]; regional differences in preferred prosthesis types (USA vs Europe) suggest no single dominant solution[3].

Source Title: Active lower limb prosthetics: a systematic review of design issues and solutions
Main Topic Area: Design methods; customization; user involvement (multiple)[4]
Key Gaps Identified: No clinical trials comparing powered vs conventional/semi-active prostheses found in engineering databases[4]; evidence relies on prototypes and small samples, needing clinical trials with commercial devices[4]; challenge to match biological actuation performance without excessive weight/size[4]; self-contained pneumatic actuation faces pressure-supply challenges (PAMs)[4].
Key Limitations Discussed: Actuation trade-offs: high force/torque, efficiency, small size, and low weight are conflicting goals[4]; echo control cannot enable asymmetric locomotion and may feel unnatural with high impedance[4]; control challenges include signal noise and high latency[4]; many concepts remain at prototyping stage (translation gap)[4].
Key Recommendations: Run larger clinical trials using commercial powered prostheses[4] across real-world tasks beyond level walking (slopes, stairs, running)[4]; explore variable-impedance actuators for smaller, powerful, more compliant devices[4].
Contradictions Or Debates: Debate on optimal knee mechanism: single-axis may be better than polycentric for active knees[4]; actuation trade-offs: electromechanical is common despite inferior power density[4], while pneumatic muscles are larger but offer higher force-to-weight and compliance[4].

Source Title: Design Optimization in Lower Limb Prostheses: A Review
Main Topic Area: Design methods (optimization, biomechanics, modeling)[8]
Key Gaps Identified: Need predictive tools to estimate user performance metrics during early design optimization[8]; over-focus on anthropomorphic designs that ignore altered post-amputation anatomy limits the solution space[8]; prosthetic joint effects on whole-body biomechanics and user experience are under-explored[8]; connecting experimental parameterization and model-based simulation to improve real-world performance remains challenging[8].
Key Limitations Discussed: Hypothesized outcomes of many designs are not consistently observed in biomechanical analyses[8]; anthropomorphic design focus constrains exploration of alternative solutions[8]; translation from experimental/simulation findings to real-world performance improvements remains difficult[8].
Key Recommendations: Incorporate predictive tools for user performance into initial design optimization[8]; pursue experimental parameterization plus model-based simulations to better predict user outcomes[8].
Contradictions Or Debates: Notes inconsistency between hypothesized benefits and observed biomechanical outcomes, indicating conflicting/inconclusive evidence across designs[8].

Source Title: Issues affecting the level of prosthetics research evidence: Secondary analysis of a systematic review
Study Type: Secondary analysis of a systematic review[10]
Main Topic Area: Design/evaluation methods (internal & external validity; reporting quality)[10]
Key Gaps Identified: Evidence quality is undermined by internal validity threats (variable comparison conditions; limited accommodation-time justification; fatigue/learning effects; lack of blinding; small samples; limited reliability evidence; attrition; weak selection-criteria reporting)[10] and external validity threats (limited sample description/representativeness; suboptimal intervention description)[10].
Key Limitations Discussed: Common limitations across prosthetics research include internal validity problems (e.g., variable comparison conditions, lack of blinding, small N, limited measurement reliability evidence)[10] and external validity problems (indeterminate representativeness; poor intervention descriptions)[10].
Key Recommendations: Calls for efforts to address methodological limitations, educate evidence consumers, and improve research reporting to advance evidence quality/use in prosthetics[10].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: User experience of transtibial prosthetic liners: A systematic review
Main Topic Area: User involvement / user experience (liners; socket–liner interaction)[7, 12]
Key Gaps Identified: Insufficient research differentiating user experience across liner types[12]; no studies used qualitative methods to systematically gather/analyze user experience[12]; intervention reporting often lacks detail, limiting synthesis confidence[12]; negative experiences are confounded by poor liner fit and poorly designed socket shapes[12].
Key Limitations Discussed: Methodological issues (sampling bias, outcome-measure validity, incorrect inferential analysis) reduce ability to distinguish experiences across liners[12]; study samples not representative of broader TTA populations[12]; early literature used non-validated questionnaires[12]; frequent use of simplistic statistics and multiple t-tests without Type I error control[12].
Key Recommendations: Recruit more representative samples (age/sex/cause/comorbidities)[12]; use more sophisticated multivariate inferential methods (requires larger samples)[12]; conduct observational and qualitative studies to identify sensitive/reliable user-experience indicators[12]; report complete descriptive & inferential statistics to enable future meta-analyses[12].
Contradictions Or Debates: Higher-quality evidence suggests elastomer liners may not improve satisfaction contrary to prevailing view[12]; some studies found small/insignificant differences between liner conditions[12]; mismatch between PEQ results and user preferences (e.g., Pelite) suggests outcome-measure sensitivity concerns[12].

Source Title: User-Centered Prosthetic Development: Comprehension of Amputees’ Needs
Study Type: Questionnaire-based user-centered study / discussion paper (with literature-review elements)[7]
Main Topic Area: User involvement; design methods; customization (multiple)[15]
Key Gaps Identified: No data on whether satisfaction is defined differently (qualitatively vs quantitatively) across amputation types[15]; missing data for lower-limb amputees regarding whether UCD can address multi-factorial satisfaction challenges[15]; further studies needed to prove whether the concept prevents incongruence/resignation[15].
Key Limitations Discussed: Some patients remain unsatisfied with their prosthesis[15]; major issues include socket fit, mechanical function, non-mechanical qualities, and support/advice for adaptation[15]; reported benefits may not translate into increased daily activity levels[15]; satisfaction is multi-causal and may include acceptance of dissatisfaction/resignation[15]; gait-speed changes correlate negatively with perceived certainty/stability[15].
Key Recommendations: Use holistic UCD where user experience/assessment is considered throughout development[15]; employ Prosthesis-User-in-the-Loop simulation concepts to integrate users into development[15]; conduct further studies to validate impact on incongruence/resignation[15].
Contradictions Or Debates: Notes incongruent correlations between self-reported satisfaction and lived problems (e.g., swelling) suggesting possible resignation/measurement issues[15]; short-term perceived benefits of advanced knees may not be reflected in real-world activity levels[15].

Source Title: Strength deficits in lower limb prosthesis users: A scoping review
Main Topic Area: Physical conditioning & strength assessment (implications for prosthesis users)[17]
Key Gaps Identified: Need alternative strength metrics and clinical tests plus research on causal links between strength deficits and functional impairments[17]; literature on muscle weakness is emerging but had not been summarized (prompting the scoping review)[17].
Key Limitations Discussed: Only 12 of 377 identified publications met inclusion criteria (limited eligible evidence base)[17]; while evidence indicates strength deficits, broader generalizability and causal inference remain constrained by the small included set[17].
Key Recommendations: More research on alternative strength metrics/clinical tests and causal links to functional impairment[17]; greater clinical and scientific attention to physical conditioning of lower-limb prosthesis users[17].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: Guidelines and Recommendations to Investigate the Efficacy of a Lower-Limb Prosthetic Device: A Systematic Review
Main Topic Area: Design methods & evaluation protocols / outcome measures (multiple)[7]
Key Gaps Identified: No standardized experimental methodology exists for evaluating lower-limb prosthetic devices, complicating cross-study comparison[19]; outcome selection is highly heterogeneous (43 outcome measures across biomechanical/physiological/physical performance/psychological domains)[19]; limited inclusion of daily activities, with recommendation to incorporate them in case reports then RCTs[19].
Key Limitations Discussed: Evaluations over-emphasize walking tests (78%), with fewer studies on slopes, stairs, or other functional tasks, limiting ecological validity and comparability[19].
Key Recommendations: Include daily activities in early case reports and later randomized controlled studies[19]; use multiple outcome domains (biomechanical, physiological, physical performance, psychological) in LLPD evaluation frameworks[19].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: Functionality and Comfort Design of Lower-Limb Prosthetics: A Review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (comfort/socket; accessibility & cost; user-centered design; neural/sensory integration)[21]
Key Gaps Identified: Calls for stronger user involvement (user-centric approach, incorporating feedback/preferences)[21]; affordability/accessibility remain major gaps needing cost-effective solutions[21]; neural interfaces and sensory feedback create unresolved opportunities/challenges for natural control/sensation[21].
Key Limitations Discussed: High cost of advanced technologies and need for specialized training/customization burden adoption[21]; long-term performance/durability remains a concern[21]; persistent socket discomfort and skin irritation[21].
Key Recommendations: Prioritize affordability and long-term performance while advancing neural integration using user-centered design approaches[21]; further R&D to enhance motor control and sensory perception[21].
Contradictions Or Debates: Tension between rapid technical advances (power/control/sensors)[21] and practical barriers (cost, training, ongoing customization)[21].

Source Title: Toward the Development of User-Centered Neurointegrated Lower Limb Prostheses
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods; customization; user needs; neurointegration/control)[22]
Key Gaps Identified: Despite advances, deficiencies remain and even the most capable prostheses fall short of healthy-limb capabilities[22]; deficiencies across components relative to users’ needs persist[22]; presents a roadmap of patient-related issues to enable next-generation neurally integrated prostheses[22].
Key Limitations Discussed: Upgrades across components have not eliminated deficiencies, and high-end prostheses still fall short of healthy-limb function[22].
Key Recommendations: Target research opportunities in design/control to address each deficiency[22] and follow a patient-centered roadmap of issues to be addressed[22].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: Focusing Research Efforts on the Unique Needs of Women Prosthesis Users
Main Topic Area: Customization; user involvement; accessibility (women-specific needs)[7]
Key Gaps Identified: Lack of solutions enabling women to wear varied footwear (including high heels)[25]; need research on footwear preferences and effects of prosthesis–footwear–limb loss on mobility/community participation[26]; women remain underserved in prosthetics research, limiting rehabilitation guidance[25].
Key Limitations Discussed: Women experience greater dissatisfaction with fit, appearance, and footwear options[25]; evidence base and prescription guidance are limited despite needs being emphasized in literature/guidelines[25]; research exploring women-specific prescription factors and footwear solutions is only beginning[25].
Key Recommendations: Targeted research to characterize footwear preferences and impacts on outcomes[25]; develop solutions expanding footwear options[25]; generate evidence-based, patient-centered prescription guidelines responsive to women’s needs[25].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: Towards Including End-Users in the Design of Prosthetic Hands: Ethical Analysis of a Survey of Australians with Upper-Limb Difference
Study Type: Survey-based literature discussion paper (hybrid: survey + critical discussion/review)[28]
Main Topic Area: User involvement (secondary: customization, design methods, accessibility)[7]
Key Gaps Identified: Few studies investigate user experience/preferences; those that do focus mainly on functional satisfaction/dissatisfaction[29]; further work needed on how to engage potential users in research/design processes[29]; paucity of population data (Australian upper-limb different population) limits representativeness judgments[29]; richer qualitative methods are needed for engineering/design questions to advance user engagement[29].
Key Limitations Discussed: Non-use can signal misfit between prosthetic designs and intended recipients[29]; more sophisticated tech does not necessarily increase uptake[29]; study limitations include small, self-selected sample[29] and question framing that may have shaped responses[29].
Key Recommendations: Incorporate user engagement into design processes and develop better engagement methods[29]; frame design as supporting users’ relational autonomy[29]; enable high customizability at point of supply due to diverse aesthetic preferences[29]; use richer qualitative methods to deepen user engagement[29].
Contradictions Or Debates: Debate over framing non-use (design problem vs user response vs non-problematic for some)[29]; empirical tension that higher-tech devices don’t necessarily improve uptake[29].

Source Title: Haptic Feedback Systems for Lower-Limb Prosthetic Applications: A Review of System Design, User Experience, and Clinical Insights
Main Topic Area: Multiple (system design; user experience; customization; clinical effectiveness)[36]
Key Gaps Identified: No comprehensive comparison of feedback modality effectiveness across limbs is available[36]; lack of standardization in actuator configurations/intensity/modalities drives inconsistent performance/outcomes[36]; lack of long-term clinical efficacy/usability data[36]; no consensus on intensity measurement/calibration methods[36]; limited comparative studies of adaptation in new vs experienced users[36].
Key Limitations Discussed: Many studies have small samples and are lab-based (limited generalizability)[36]; invasive approaches face surgical risks, high cost, and signal-clarity complexity[36]; mechanotactile feedback can require bulky actuators, limiting use in compact/lightweight prostheses[36]; vibrotactile adaptation can reduce effectiveness over time[36]; complex feedback can cause cognitive overload[36].
Key Recommendations: Run longitudinal real-world studies over weeks/months assessing accuracy, reaction times, durability, adoption, and overall effectiveness[36]; develop adaptable, intuitive, standardized haptic systems[36]; emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration and user-centered design for feedback modality advances[36].
Contradictions Or Debates: Sequential vs simultaneous vibrotactile pattern presentation: simultaneous may be faster but risks confusion[36], while sequential can yield higher accuracy[36].

Source Title: A Systematic Review of Natural Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites in Prosthetic Socket Fabrication
Main Topic Area: Materials & customization (socket fabrication)[39]
Key Gaps Identified: Need clinical comparative analyses of NFRP vs conventional socket materials to understand performance trade-offs[38]; preliminary user feedback is encouraging but broader studies are needed to establish user satisfaction[38]; need to bridge research-to-clinical-practice for implementation[38]; further optimization of fiber types/orientations/treatments to improve strength/durability/flexibility[38].
Key Limitations Discussed: Variability in fiber properties (length, orientation, moisture) affects consistency of composites[38], making quality control critical[38]; accessibility and cost considerations may limit adoption[38]; integration requires specialized training/expertise[38].
Key Recommendations: Develop advanced formulations to enhance material properties[38]; integrate NFRP with other emerging technologies for innovation[38]; prioritize translational work bridging research and clinical practice[38]; pursue multidisciplinary collaboration among material scientists, engineers, and clinicians for adoption[38].
Contradictions Or Debates: Trade-off debate: conventional materials often have superior strength/light weight, while NFRP may offer biocompatibility and potentially reduced cost[38].

Source Title: Technology for monitoring everyday prosthesis use: a systematic review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods; customization; accessibility; user involvement via acceptability/feedback)[40]
Key Gaps Identified: Limited objective data on prosthesis wear time, tasks performed, and design adjustments that improve usefulness in-context[40]; few studies monitor use beyond step counts or classify activity types[40]; monitoring durations are short and there are no longitudinal studies (>1 month typical max)[40]; evidence on designing/distributing accessible/affordable prostheses that meet user needs is lacking[40]; user acceptability of actimeters is not reported[40].
Key Limitations Discussed: Sensor cost, limited battery life, and limited availability prevent routine clinical use in many countries[40]; small sample size is common due to recruitment challenges[40]; community studies often measure only steps/min or steps/day[40]; analysis algorithms are not user-friendly and require programming/signal-processing skills[40]; broader barriers include cost, access, training/capacity, and technical/cultural issues[40].
Key Recommendations: Use monitoring alongside clinical scores and user feedback to assess whether prostheses meet requirements[40]; develop algorithms to detect activity types from sensors (e.g., below-knee placement)[40]; develop shared datasets with metadata standards for cross-study comparison and early warning of socket/tissue issues[40]; create synchronized frameworks for out-of-clinic monitoring suited to low-resource contexts[40]; select sensors that allow access to raw data[40].
Contradictions Or Debates: Component-comparison studies often find no clinically significant differences, possibly due to small samples/insensitive outcomes (not true equivalence)[40]; studies on prosthetic feet report significant differences while many other component comparisons do not[40]; clinical ambulation ability may not match real-world ambulation levels, challenging outcome validity[40].

Source Title: A review of user needs to drive the development of lower limb prostheses
Main Topic Area: Multiple (user needs; assessment; sensory feedback; social participation)[41]
Key Gaps Identified: Need–performance–QoL relationship remains open (specific needs vs objective performance vs satisfaction/QoL)[41]; unknown how to address social integration, sexual activity, acceptance, appearance, battery life, and clothing/shoe restrictions[41]; lack of commercially available artificial sensory feedback solutions[41]; prosthesis types are poorly reported in included references, limiting generalizability[41].
Key Limitations Discussed: User needs are multifaceted, context-dependent, and interact with each other and overall experience/QoL, complicating design translation[41]; current assessment methods likely insufficient, motivating new approaches[41]; self-reported outcomes often do not correlate with objective function measures[41]; clinical gait analyses are not representative of real-world performance[41].
Key Recommendations: Treat identifying user needs as critical for next-gen LLP development[41]; consider additional assessment/development factors and heterogeneous responses across users[41]; combine objective measures with individuals’ impressions and account for inter-subject differences[41]; explore neural correlates (e.g., cortical activity) as potential assessment tools for cognitive load/function[41].
Contradictions Or Debates: Subjective confidence may improve without objective fall reduction (balance confidence up; stumbles/falls not significantly down)[41]; recurrent mismatch between self-reported outcomes and objective function measures[41].

Source Title: Effects of lower limb prosthesis on activity, participation, and quality of life: a systematic review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (daily life, activity/participation, quality of life)[42]
Key Gaps Identified: Lack of knowledge on how prosthesis systems affect daily life in users’ natural contexts[42]; inconsistent results and variable study quality motivate need for high-quality effectiveness studies on daily living & QoL[42]; key factors influencing effectiveness on users’ everyday life remain under-studied[42].
Key Limitations Discussed: Evidence base is limited by small number of studies, varying quality, diverse prosthetic systems, and diverse outcome instruments[42]; few participants and short follow-up times[42]; internal validity varies and few studies meet longer follow-up criteria (>4 months)[42].
Key Recommendations: Gather complementary evidence on device effectiveness to enrich clinical practice[42]; conduct high-quality studies reflecting effectiveness in daily living and QoL[42]; prioritize research on key factors affecting effectiveness in everyday life[42].
Contradictions Or Debates: Findings on microprocessor knees (MPK) vs non-MPK are inconsistent: QoL/use may improve while activity/participation/satisfaction results vary across studies[42].

Source Title: Lower-Limb Prosthetic Technologies in the Developing World: A Review of Literature from 1994–2010
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods; customization/socket fit; accessibility in low-resource contexts)[43]
Key Gaps Identified: Urgent need for research, development, and evaluation of appropriate orthopaedic technology[43]; more R&D required[43]; little new information on some key issues[43]; no studies found on socket suspension technologies specifically for developing countries[43]; dissemination barriers may restrict publication of in-country R&D in peer-reviewed literature[43].
Key Limitations Discussed: Common limitations include inadequate durability of prosthetic feet[43], poor socket fit[43], and poor alignment[43]; CAD/CAM has high investment/maintenance costs limiting suitability[43]; achieving good socket fit requires well-trained personnel[43]; more biomechanically sophisticated devices may be more likely to break down (durability trade-off)[43].
Key Recommendations: Develop lightweight foot components with improved durability (including cosmetic shell)[43]; perform independent field trials for complex technologies in developing countries[43]; promote collaboration between developed and developing country teams to enable high-quality, clinically relevant, publishable work[43]; ensure publications cover technical development, clinical assessment, and field trials[43].
Contradictions Or Debates: Explicit tension: improve biomechanical performance but not at the expense of durability[43]; evidence that high-end methods (e.g., CAD/CAM) are substantially better than conventional approaches is limited[43]; designing for developing countries involves conflicting requirements (cost, durability, performance, appropriateness)[43].

Source Title: Adjustable prosthetic sockets: a systematic review of industrial and research design characteristics and their justifications
Main Topic Area: Customization (adjustable sockets); design methods; accessibility/low-resource settings; industry–academia translation (multiple)[44]
Key Gaps Identified: Design–comfort/function relationships are rarely investigated (major gap)[44]; clear difference between commercial vs research design approaches (panels/circumferential vs bladders)[44]; weak reporting/justification for adjustment locations/ranges[44]; limited investigation of what defines a well-fitting socket[44]; many commercial designs lack published clinical support (68.75%)[44]; few studies address low-resource settings (only one low-resource study)[44].
Key Limitations Discussed: Clinical studies are generally small; only 17.6% assessed a commercially available socket[44]; many adjustable sockets lack safety features preventing over/under-tightening (tissue damage / inadequate coupling risks)[44]; majority of clinical evidence is small case/cohort studies[44]; adverse events underreported (5 of 34 participant studies)[44]; review limitation: no physical inspection of sockets, requiring assumptions about adjustment mechanisms[44].
Key Recommendations: Prioritize research on adjustable socket suitability globally, especially in low-resource settings[44]; improve researcher–industry knowledge exchange[44]; study relationships between socket design, mechanical coupling, comfort, and residual-limb tissue health[44]; assess comfort at different adjustment levels/locations[44]; use scientific methods to compare design groups and identify which patient subgroups benefit most[44].
Contradictions Or Debates: Industry vs research focus differs, creating uncertainty about best designs[44]; comfort improvements are often reported but not well explained/quantified[44]; some benefits shown with motor-driven panel actuation may not translate to conventional mechanisms[44].

Source Title: Design, Kinematics and Gait Analysis, of Prosthetic Knee Joints: A Systematic Review
Main Topic Area: Design methods; kinematics; gait & control (multiple)[7]
Key Gaps Identified: Need powered knee joints that meet amputees’ requirements[45]; uphill/inclined ambulation remains difficult and needs investigation[45]; intent recognition for stairs (height/cadence, etc.) remains unaddressed in much prior work[45]; active EMG-based transfemoral prostheses remain challenging[45]; many studies lack real-time amputee testing (models/healthy subjects/virtual environments)[45].
Key Limitations Discussed: Commercial prosthetic legs are not reliable/comfortable enough[45]; many use fixed-impedance hydraulic/pneumatic components that cannot adapt across locomotion situations[45]; active/powered prostheses are complex and often not tested in real-time scenarios with amputees[45]; material constraints exist (e.g., CFRP poor electrical conductivity for active systems)[45].
Key Recommendations: Design EMG-based electromechanical transfemoral prostheses for intent recognition and impedance/torque control[45]; test in real-time scenarios (beyond models/virtual/healthy subjects)[45]; provide user training to improve adaptation[45].
Contradictions Or Debates: Trade-offs noted: hybrid passive/active designs may reduce stability[45]; microprocessor-controlled prostheses generally perform better than non-microprocessor-controlled ones[45], yet achieving stable volitional control is tied to closed-loop active control needs[45].

Source Title: Improving access to prosthetic limbs in Germany: An explorative review
Main Topic Area: Accessibility (care pathways, reimbursement, regulation) with user-centered design implications[46]
Key Gaps Identified: Service users face hurdles to obtaining suitable prostheses (waiting times; pressure to negotiate need), highlighting access gaps[46]; access and distribution of innovations could be improved via organizational/regulatory measures[46]; need integrated approaches including user-centered design, health technology assessment, care-pathway monitoring, and societal discussion of rationing[46].
Key Limitations Discussed: Stakeholder views on reimbursement issues sometimes conflict, indicating systemic friction and lack of shared criteria[46]; practical access barriers include waiting times and user burden to negotiate device needs[46].
Key Recommendations: Implement organizational and regulatory measures to improve equitable access and innovation distribution[46]; consider user-centered design, health technology assessment, monitoring of care pathways, and societal discussion on rationing[46].
Contradictions Or Debates: Reports conflicting stakeholder perspectives on prosthetic reimbursement processes and needs[46].

Source Title: Upper Limb Prostheses by the Level of Amputation: A Systematic Review
Main Topic Area: Multiple (design methods, customization, accessibility, user involvement)[50]
Key Gaps Identified: Commercialization/maturation gap: absence of technologies at TRL 8 across categories[50]; few studies use EEG control alone or combined with EMG[50]; little research focused on weight reduction[50]; need scalable personalization for specific levels (e.g., transmetacarpal/transcarpal) which require personalized forms[50]; limited evidence on certifications/approvals, especially for non-established brands[50]; major accessibility gap given most upper-limb amputees live in developing countries[50].
Key Limitations Discussed: Durability issues in soft-material designs (wear after ~6 months)[50]; design limitations reduce mobility in uncontrolled environments[50]; physiological control signals can be scarce/attenuated at higher levels of amputation[50]; translational gap reflected in lack of TRL-8 devices[50]; limited information on pediatric prostheses[50].
Key Recommendations: Prioritize prosthesis weight reduction[50]; strengthen designer–user collaboration to improve ownership/embodiment[50]; develop richer haptics (pressure plus temperature/texture/slip)[50]; focus on bridging the commercialization gap[50].
Contradictions Or Debates: Control-modality debate: surface EMG predominates[50] but FMG is argued to be cheaper/more accurate/more consistent[50].

Source Title: A scoping review on upper extremity prostheses: Satisfaction, barriers, and their implications in resource-limited countries
Main Topic Area: Accessibility; user involvement (satisfaction); customization (resource-limited settings)[51]
Key Gaps Identified: Abandonment rates are not well understood in resource-limited countries[51]; insufficient research on how prosthesis characteristics (type/comfort/weight/functionality/price/availability) and individual factors shape adherence/satisfaction in these settings[51].
Key Limitations Discussed: Evidence base is thin: 425 studies identified but only 7 cross-sectional studies included[51]; barriers include device characteristics and patient factors (e.g., comfort/price/availability; pain; time to fitting), limiting generalizable design guidance[51].
Key Recommendations: Tailored prosthetic design and funding may improve adherence[51].
Contradictions Or Debates: Not mentioned in source.

Source Title: A Review: Aesthetic element in prosthetic’s cosmetic design for lower limb physical amputees
Main Topic Area: Design methods; customization; user involvement (aesthetics/cosmesis)[52]
Key Gaps Identified: Most prior research is not artistic/design-oriented[52]; critical need to incorporate design-centered and user-centered approaches that include aesthetics, comfort, and usability[52].
Key Limitations Discussed: Review-method limitations: reliance on Google Scholar may constrain comprehensiveness[52]; temporal scope confined to 2018–2024[52]; reliance on English-dominant databases introduces bias and may exclude non-English studies[52]; broader field limitation: past research emphasized function (clinical/engineering) at the expense of user satisfaction[52].
Key Recommendations: Adopt design-centered, user-centered research including aesthetics, comfort, and usability[52]; broaden database selection and extend publication period to reduce language bias and improve comprehensiveness[52]; encourage collaboration with artists/fashion experts to support identity/expressive prosthesis design[52].
Contradictions Or Debates: Frames an ongoing transition from function-first paradigms to user-focused interdisciplinary design culture[52].
